THOUGHT: This 30-year-old male presents with acute-onset left-sided chest pain, productive cough with purulent sputum, shortness of breath, fever (38.7°C), and malaise — all evolving over one week following recent influenza infection. His hypoxemia is severe (SpO₂ 80% on room air), indicating significant respiratory compromise. Physical exam reveals classic signs of focal pneumonia: dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds, and crackles at the left lung base. Chest X-ray confirms alveolar infiltrates with air bronchograms in the left lower lobe — hallmark radiographic features of bacterial consolidation. Lab findings show leukocytosis (12,000/mm³) with marked neutrophilia (82%), consistent with bacterial infection. The recent influenza infection is a critical risk factor for post-viral bacterial pneumonia — particularly *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in otherwise healthy adults. His young age, non-smoking status, and absence of comorbidities make atypical pathogens (e.g., *Mycoplasma*) or chronic lung disease less likely; however, the severity (hypoxemia, systemic toxicity, lobar consolidation) strongly favors typical bacterial etiology. While viral or atypical pneumonias can occur post-influenza, the purulent sputum, neutrophilic leukocytosis, lobar consolidation with air bronchograms, and clinical severity are most consistent with bacterial superinfection — specifically community-acquired lobar pneumonia.

DIAGNOSIS: Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia
